inline.alt: Broken shackles and chain.
inline.caption: Broken shackles. Quran 90:13 lists the freeing of a slave, and 24:33 tells owners to write contracts of freedom.

inline.alt: A glowing tent under the Milky Way in a desert at night.
inline.caption: A desert night. On the road to Medina the Prophet ﷺ covered her with a cloak (Bukhari 2235); the photograph is not of that road.

featured.alt: An old photo album with retro photographs.
featured.caption: An old photo album. A testimony is good evidence of what happened to the person who tells it.

inline.alt: Elderly hands holding a small framed photograph of a man.
inline.caption: Elderly hands holding a photograph. People who suffered in a household that called itself Muslim should be believed.

inline.alt: A farmers market with stalls of produce.
inline.caption: A market with many stalls. A collection chosen from those who left is a sample of one kind of story.

inline.alt: A door ajar with a thin line of light in a dark room.
inline.caption: A door ajar. The root of "Islam" and of "peace" is the same in Arabic (s-l-m).

featured.alt: A pair of hands typing on a laptop beside a cup of coffee.
featured.caption: Typing a reply. The Quran asks a Muslim to answer provocation with what is better (41:34).

inline.alt: The painted domed ceiling and arches inside a mosque.
inline.caption: A mosque interior, a stock picture. Pew counted about 1.8 billion Muslims in 2015, nearly a quarter of the world.

inline.alt: A market stall hung with colourful fabrics and textiles.
inline.caption: A market stall of fabrics, a stock picture. The Quran's reason for the outer garment is that women "will be known and not be abused" (33:59).

inline.alt: A lit candle among dark roses.
inline.caption: A candle among roses. Fifty-one people were killed in two Christchurch mosques on 15 March 2019.

featured.alt: Rows of seats in an empty lecture hall.
featured.caption: A lecture hall. Nine questions from the floor of a debate on the Islamic dilemma.

inline.alt: A scroll with Hebrew writing beside a quill and an ink pot.
inline.caption: A scroll and a quill, a stock picture. The Quran speaks of people who write the "scripture" with their own hands (2:79); it names no date or council.

inline.alt: A close view of a Hebrew Torah scroll.
inline.caption: A Hebrew scroll, a stock picture. Verse 10:94 tells the Prophet to ask those who have been reading the Scripture before him.

inline.alt: A crescent moon in a dark blue sky.
inline.caption: A crescent moon. The moon-god theory has no support in the evidence cited, and Arabic-speaking Christians use the word Allah.

inline.alt: A knotted rope.
inline.caption: A knotted rope. A covenant that replaces and a covenant that confirms are not one thing.

featured.alt: The Ten Commandments on two stone tablets in a garden beside a brick wall.
featured.caption: The Ten Commandments on stone tablets, a stock picture. Jeremiah 31 promises a law written in the heart, and Deuteronomy 30:6 had already promised a circumcised heart.

inline.alt: A hand holding a red glass heart against a black background.
inline.caption: A hand holding a heart, a stock picture. "I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart" (Jeremiah 31:33).

inline.alt: A page of old handwritten Latin text.
inline.caption: A page of an old manuscript, a stock picture. Joshua, Josiah and Nehemiah each made a covenant with the people around the same book.

inline.alt: An old open book with a pair of spectacles beside a lit lantern.
inline.caption: An old book by candlelight, a stock picture. Hebrews 8:13 reads Jeremiah's "new" as making the first covenant old.

inline.alt: Olive branches with green leaves against a wooden frame and a blue sky.
inline.caption: Olive branches, a stock picture. The Quran has covenants with Israel, the Christians, the prophets and the believers.

featured.alt: A man leading three camels across a desert under a stormy sky.
featured.caption: A desert caravan, a stock picture. The Quran addresses Quraysh as a people of the winter and summer caravans (106:2).

inline.alt: A sailing ship on a stormy sea under dark clouds.
inline.caption: A ship in a storm, a stock picture. "When they board a ship, they supplicate Allāh, sincere to Him in religion" (29:65).

inline.alt: Ruined stone arches and columns lit by the low sun.
inline.caption: Ancient ruins, a stock picture, not a Meccan site. The Quran calls al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt names with no authority behind them (53:23).

inline.alt: A horse running across sand dunes in a desert.
inline.caption: A horse in a desert, a stock picture. The sources for what the Meccans believed are the Quran and Muslim reports, since no Meccan text survives.

inline.alt: A thin crescent moon in a dark night sky.
inline.caption: A crescent moon, a stock picture. "Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allāh, who created them" (41:37).

featured.alt: A page of the Quran in early Kufic script, brown ink on parchment.
featured.caption: A folio of the Quran in Kufic script, Egypt, Abbasid period. The changes of grammatical person discussed here run through every copy of the text.

inline.alt: Two pages of a handwritten Arabic commentary, black ink on paper.
inline.caption: A fragment of al-Zamakhshari's commentary on the Quran, al-Kashshaf (Bibliothèque nationale de France, Arabe 6313). He explained iltifat from the opening pages of his commentary.

inline.alt: A column of rain falls from a cloud over a calm bay at sunset.
inline.caption: A rain shaft at sunset, seen from Man-of-War Bay (NOAA). In the verses on rain the Quran turns to "We" at the point where the land is given life (27:60; 35:9).

inline.alt: Large Kufic letters in brown ink with red vowel dots on parchment.
inline.caption: A folio of the Quran in Kufic script with part of 48:27–28, Abbasid period (Freer Gallery of Art, F1930.62).

inline.alt: A double page of the opening chapter of the Quran in gold script, framed in blue and gold illumination.
inline.caption: The opening chapter in the Quran of Baybars al-Jashnakir, Cairo, 1304–1306 (British Library, Add MS 22406). The left page begins "You alone we worship", where the prayer turns to address God (1:5).
inline.artist: Muhammad ibn al-Wahid (copyist); Abu Bakr Sandal and others (illumination)

featured.alt: Crumbling mud-brick walls among the ruins of ancient Babylon, under a pale sky.
featured.caption: The ruins of Babylon, photographed by the Matson Photo Service in the 1930s. The Quran names Babylon as the place where the two angels Harut and Marut were sent as a trial (2:102).
featured.artist: Matson Photo Service (G. Eric and Edith Matson Photograph Collection, Library of Congress)

inline.alt: A handwritten Arabic page in black and red ink, with some phrases underlined in red.
inline.caption: A page of al-Tabari's History of the Prophets and Kings (Fazil Ahmed Pasha Library, 1043). Jung draws many of his Muslim stories from al-Tabari's reports. The red underlining was added by the uploader.

inline.alt: An open printed volume of the Talmud, Hebrew text in columns around a central block.
inline.caption: The Babylonian Talmud, Seder Zera'im, printed by Daniel Bomberg in Venice, 1543 to 1544. Jung's first witness for the angels' objection is the Talmud, Sanhedrin 38b.

inline.alt: An open parchment manuscript with two pages of Syriac script in brown ink.
inline.caption: Ephrem's Commentary on the Diatessaron in Syriac, Egypt, late fifth or early sixth century (Chester Beatty Library). The Cave of Treasures, which Jung cites for Satan's refusal, was written in Syriac in about the same period.

inline.alt: A deep trench cut between mud-brick walls in the ruins of Babylon, with a man standing at the top.
inline.caption: An underground chamber in the ruins of Babylon, 1930s. Later Muslim storytellers placed Harut and Marut in a pit at Babylon; the Quran says nothing of a pit, a fall or a woman.
inline.artist: Matson Photo Service (G. Eric and Edith Matson Photograph Collection, Library of Congress)
